segments.text: All right, joining me now is Maharashtra FDA Commissioner, Mr. Tukaram Munde.
Mr. Munde, thank you for taking the time out and joining us.
Mr. Munde, when you exposed the markups, which are as high as nearly 3000% on hospital consumables, you haven't really even touched a raw nerve.
You've spoken up for the armed army of this country who has to face this day in and day out.
What made you speak on this issue, sir?
See, the issue is not about speaking for just consumers, but as a regulator, it's my job.
It's my role to look at the issues.

And the issue here is about market prices of the consumers which are consumed in the hospital, particularly in IPD, whether it's IV sets or whether it's nebulizers or other consumables which are used daily basis for IPD purposes.
Now we conducted based on some inputs and complaints that there are a lot of discrepancies in the MRP price and actually the hospital price plus billing.
So we conducted a survey across MMR regions and other hospitals where we found that there have been differences in MRP and actually the price at which the hospital gets that product.
So we have found anywhere in the range of 150% to almost 2800% difference between MRP and the trade price at which the hospital procures.
But the benefit is not passed on to the consumer.
It is either with the hospital or with the pharmaceutical industry or the manufacturer or dealer, whoever the case may be.
So that is not felt at practice in a real sense, it is not a transparency.
So as per the prevailing rules, we have taken up the issue with the appropriate authority, that is NPPA in this context.
So we have sent a proposal to the NPPA.

enumerating the discrepancies which we have found, the gaps which we have found, the market price, MRP and the actual practices and we have submitted certain recommendations to look it up into the issue including inter-agency review, including fair trade prices, including fair trade margins and of course transparency to be brought up in.

So, we are aware within the right as a regulator, I have to look into the issues, whatever the issues come up with me, and we have taken up the issue with the appropriate authority, who is a competent authority in this sector.
Sir, it's well within your rights to take it up, but rarely has any authority ever spoken about this, though there have been consumer forums across many years who've constantly brought this issue up.

When you say, sir, and you, you know, Mr. Munde, you've tweeted this out, you've basically used a social media platform to put this out, and you write a review of these findings and clear guidelines on the permissible gap,
between trade procurement price and declared MRP has been recommended to the Department of Pharmaceuticals and the NPPA.
A step towards closing not just the pricing gap but the information gap patients are left to bear alone.
How are you going to follow up with what you have written to the NPPA and the Department of Pharmaceuticals?
Because there has always been a lot of resistance and there is a massive pharma lobby, especially where even private hospitals are concerned.
I believe that we have to look it up in the holistic issue.
It's not lobby or say the consumer lobby versus pharma lobby or hospital lobby versus a regulator, something is not like that.
We have to look at it in 360 degree context.
Pharmacy product producers are there, manufacturers are there, they have their IP rights, they produce it, but the trade margin has to be reasonable.
As per NPPA we have what we call essential commodities act and there is a DPCO order which is revised from time to time.
The current DPCO order is 2013 and in that order essential medicines are defined, their MRP is also looked into.
Beyond that, there are certain items which every year pharma companies or manufacturers are allowed to increase by a particular percentage point of view.
While fixing a pricing or MRP, there is a process defined in it.
But when we look at this type of margins, which is to the tune of 2,800, I think that is not acceptable to anybody, whether as a regulator or as a consumer or a citizen, it's not allowed.

Now, why does a particular product which is sold to a particular hospital at a particular say 11 rupees rate whose MRP is 325 odd rupees, it is really inexplicable to me, it is very very revealing to me that why this gap exists.

if they can sell at 11 rupees then why can't it be a MRP of a particular around that rupees maybe 10 percent 20 percent 25 percent of margin why it takes to be 2800 percent odd to cap that MRP and I think this is the exactly issue we have raised up after our findings and that's why we have taken up the appropriate forum and authority Mr.Munde are you proposing a cap or a fixed price for
these hospital consumables what is permissible limit like you yourself say certain hospitals they have markups up to 2800 and even over is what we've also figured out so are you proposing a cap
So I am not proposing any cap say because the caps will be decided, MRP will be decided from product to product basis.
Now how much the margin should be there while deciding MRP it has to be rational, it has to be open, it has to be transparent.
There cannot be this much gap.
This is inexplicable.

That's where we have suggested certain things, whether that should be brought under DPCO or that should be trade margins have to be decided or whether there has to be interagency coordination has to be there.
And the pricing monitoring mechanism has to be strengthened.
There are certain four or five recommendations we have given.
But it is for the authority to look into.
They will go consult all the stakeholders in the sector, whether it's a pharmacy industry, whether it's a hospital, whether it's a regulators, whether it's a consumers.
And after deliberation, consultations, NPPA will come up with appropriate interventions.
That's what we have requested.
There has to be intervention.
There seems to be a gap, along with the regulatory gap, policy gap, and interventions are required.
And we have taken up the issue.
We have brushed up the issue.
And I believe that with the deliberation in a transparent manner, that this issue will be addressed.
have you given a time limit for this issue to be addressed sir because a lot of these recommendations and reviews go into a cold box.

I am not authoritative to give a time limit to the author, I am not authoritative to give time limit to NPPA, NPPA is the one who will decide it but of course there have been discussion, there have been interaction and I think these interactions and discussions are on positive note.
Sir, most private hospitals say that what you suggest is far off from the economic realities of running a private hospital.
Like when you walk into a hotel, there are certain services that you pay for.
For these hospitals, they suggest to keep a sanitized atmosphere to have round-the-clock nursing and other exigency costs that are related to the hospital.
These markups help them to offset the costs of
See, when this is to be done, that will be done in consultation and discussion with the pharma industry itself.
It is not going to be done by me.
It is going to be done by national authority.
And while arriving at a decision or if there is going to be intervention, that definitely will be discussed with hospitals as well and the pharmacy industry as well.
It is not going to be unilateral decision.
It's not going to be arbitrary decision.
And that decision does not lie with me.
and I will not be able to comment to what price, how much, what intervention will be done because that is for policy, that's a policy level matter and policy level decision will be taken.
But just to say that because we are running hospital, we are aware of where you are running hospital, but there has to be explanation for each and everything.
If a particular product
is MRP 320 odd rupees, is being sold to hospital 11 rupees, the same product which is outside will get at the same price, where is this margin going?
That is the valid question to be asked by either the consumer or a regulator for that matter.
As this matter approached up to me, we looked into it, we studied it, we surveyed it and we found there is some rationale in it, this needs to be addressed, this needs to be, we need answers on this.

and that's why we have taken it up with the appropriate authority and I believe that with due deliberations whatever is the right approach will have to be followed because pharmacy industry or manufacturer will not work in white, hospitals will not work in white, at the same time consumer will also not be working in white.
They will not also be taken for right.
So as per Drug and Control Act and rules they are under, this is a major legislation along with the Essential Commodity Act.
Other legislations also need to be taken into account including consumer interest.
We cannot just take that we are running the hospital.
That's what we are entitled for this.
What we need is a transparency.
What we need is ethical practices, both from manufacturers, hospitals, as well as the consumers, along with legal practices.
So that's where our role as a regulator comes in.
That's where we have taken up the issue.
And while taking a decision, interest of all stakeholders will have to be taken into consideration.
Mr. Munde you know consumer interest has always been last in the pecking order and I am sure as a regulator you have seen that happen.
The arbitrariness of markups in hospitals you have rightly pointed out but you do understand.
It's not the first time.
A lot of consumer interest bodies have constantly bobbed this up and they've hit a wall against very very strong lobbies.
You do understand by bringing this up once again you could be in the crosshairs of certain very influential powerful bodies.
No, I am not at crossroads with anybody.
I am basically performing a role which I am expected to perform.
Being a regulator, being a public servant, that's my role.
Being FDA Commissioner of Maharashtra, Drug Administration in Maharashtra.
Whatever the issues are in drug sector, whether from drug industry side, pharmacy industry side, hospital side or consumer side.
We have to look into the issues.
This is one of the issues.
There are other issues which we have taken up about other sectors also.
So it has nothing to do against a particular lobby.
We are here as a public servant.
I am just trying to perform my role as a public servant.
That's it.
So nobody has to take it in a negative context.
We have to take it in a holistic context.

the interest of all the stakeholders including hospitals, including pharmacy industry, manufacture, including consumers and of course the government has to be taken into consideration while arriving at a decision.
Last two questions sir, you are a regulatory body and as per you, what do you think would be a fair percentage markup?
Because what you yourself said, right now you're looking at anything over 2,800.
That will be very difficult for me.
That will be very, very difficult for me to comment upon.
Because that role is of NPPA and the industry.
So they will deliberate upon it, and they will decide upon it.
I am no way authorized, nor am I expert in that.
But definitely, as a regulator, if there are issues that I have to take up, we are taking up the issues, along with many, many other issues.
Well, thank you so much, Mr. Munde, for taking it up.
Like I said, you have echoed what has been, you know, the grouse of lakhs of common men in this country where you go into hospitals and you are handed inflated bills without any explanation at all.
And you have to pay for that.
So thank you for bringing it up.
And you are right.
You said you have little control, but you have flagged it.
Let's hope that, you know,
whatever your submissions are, are taken seriously and some tangible change is made.

I just want to ask you one quick question, sir, before I let you go and that for Mumbaikas could be, you know, as sensitive for some of them who followed Mondagar Cafe through the many years and decades and you have shut it.
Now, what led you, Mr. Munde, to shut down Cafe Mondagar, which is iconic to Mumbai and South Mumbai?
It's not about, I say, a bill for me, whether it's a big or small.
I have said many times on your channel as well.
So there are violations, scheduled for violations.
There are non-compliances.
And after non-compliances are found, we have suspended the license.
We have not canceled it yet.
If they comply with that, we'll re-establish the license.
If they don't comply, we'll go for a cancellation of it.
So it's basically about the public health issue.
It is about the standards and regulations not being followed.

and detailed press note I have issued yesterday so the reasons are also mentioned therein and need not repeat it only issue is that whoever is a food business operator either a licensee or registered one please follow this regulations because we are dealing with the health of the people Mr. Muneer if I know you don't want to repeat you know what the issues were with Cafe Mondega but what was the biggest glaring issue that you said that this has there has to be a suspension letter not a warning
Schedule 4 violation is the non-negotiable thing and there are violations about schedule 4 as per the Regulations of Registration and Licensing Regulation 2011.
So schedule 4 has lot many components and they have been pointed out to them.
It is not something which is opaque, it is absolutely transparent.
In the suspension notice itself those have been pointed out which are the compliances, which are non-compliances, which are partial compliances.
It is intimated to them.
They have to come with compliances and further process will take place.
Mr. Munde, thank you so much for joining us.
You know, Cafe Mondega might be just one cafe there, but what you have raised in terms of hospital is something that is going to resonate way beyond Maharashtra.
Lacks of, you know, common middle-class families face the brunt of this.
Thank you, sir, for joining us.
Thank you.
